title: Star Trek: TOS 'Charlie X' 60th anniversary (Redshirts retro review) - NewsBreak
text:
By Calvin Townsend ,
6 hours ago Star Trek: The Original Series courtesy of Titan Books | Star Trek: The Original Series courtesy of Titan Books On paper, “Charlie X” sounds like a straightforward piece of 1960s sci-fi : a teenage boy rescued from a desolate world turns out to have terrifying powers. In practice, it’s one of the most unsettling hours of early Star Trek , precisely because its “godlike being” is painfully human. He’s not an omniscient alien; he’s a lonely, awkward kid who has never learned how to live around other people.
60 years after it first aired on Sept. 15, 1966, “Charlie X” plays like a pressure cooker about power, entitlement, and the limits of compassion. The USS Enterprise isn’t just transporting a passenger; it’s trapped with someone who can rewrite reality in a tantrum.
The episode never lets you forget that this is a child, emotionally, even as it shows exactly how dangerous childish thinking becomes when there are no boundaries to hold it in check. With that in mind, the following are five elements that make “Charlie X” worth watching even now.
1. A terrifyingly plausible omnipotence Many stories give their omnipotent characters a godlike calm or theatrical flair. “Charlie X” takes a different route: Charlie Evans is tense, defensive, needy, and painfully insecure. The episode's best horror is the clash between his raw force and his emotional age. He can erase faces, twist bodies, and make people vanish, but he still sulks like a teenager who’s been told to turn down his music.
That combination feels disturbingly plausible. The episode keeps tying his outbursts to very recognizable triggers: embarrassment in front of peers, rejection from someone he wants, and a sense that adults are “ganging up” on him.
Each time Charlie feels slighted, his response escalates from social awkwardness to supernatural retaliation. Viewed through a modern lens, it’s a chilling illustration of what happens when someone who has never learned to process frustration suddenly finds themselves with the tools to enforce their will on everyone around them.
2. An unsettling look at consent and entitlement One of the most striking aspects of “Charlie X” today is how directly it tackles consent, especially in the way Charlie fixates on Yeoman Janice Rand. From the start, Charlie decides he is entitled to her attention and affection. He interprets basic kindness as encouragement, ignores her attempts to set boundaries, and treats every interaction as proof she “belongs” to him.
The episode doesn’t sugarcoat how frightening that feels for Rand. Her discomfort is visible long before Charlie’s powers are fully revealed. She tries to redirect him gently, then more firmly, and each time he refuses to accept her autonomy. His romantic fantasies are never portrayed as sweet or harmless; they’re framed as intrusive, escalating into punishment when she doesn’t respond the way he wants.
This makes “Charlie X” a warning about entitlement, power, and consent. Charlie's fixation with Rand shows the dangerous belief that wanting someone gives you access. Telekinetic outbursts and reality-warping punishments boost coercion and emotional intimidation, turning the episode's sci-fi concept into a metaphor for how people push, control, or avenge rejection.
The episode shows how entitlement and immaturity may make someone who cannot handle rejection by externalizing Charlie's emotional instability as a godlike power.
3. The Enterprise as a fragile social ecosystem Another highlight is the episode's usage of the Enterprise as a small, close-knit community. People work, relax, and make friends on the ship. Crew members joke, share music, dine, and manage social awkwardness before the situation becomes dire.
This sense of normalcy makes Charlie's presence so disturbing. As his behavior spirals, everyday ship routines become riskier. A harmless joke, chuckle, or casual remark can cause an exaggerated, reality-bending response. Everyone's life aboard the Enterprise can be altered by one person's mood, which becomes a floating hostage situation.
In that way, the episode becomes a study of how a single unchecked individual can warp an entire environment. The stakes aren’t only whether the crew will survive physically; it’s whether they can continue to live together as a functioning community while one person refuses to abide by the same rules as everyone else.
4. Kirk as moral teacher & reluctant parental figure “Charlie X” also offers an intriguing glimpse of James T. Kirk beyond captain and action hero. Here, he’s positioned as Charlie’s primary role model, the adult whose approval the boy craves and whose behavior he tries to imitate. That dynamic makes Kirk something like an unwilling father figure, tasked with teaching morality to someone who can rewrite reality whenever he’s displeased.
The episode doesn’t pretend this is easy. Kirk isn’t instantly wise or perfectly patient; he misreads Charlie at first and underestimates the danger. But once Kirk understands what he’s dealing with, his approach isn’t just to outmaneuver Charlie tactically.
Kirk tries to explain why certain behaviors are unacceptable, why desire doesn’t confer ownership, and why living among others demands self-control. His “you don’t have the right” attitude toward Charlie’s use of power is as important as any strategy on the bridge.
Kirk is shown as an admirable leader who recognizes that setting an example of accountability is just as important as giving orders. Kirk is not just trying to defend his ship; he's trying to convince a child that just because you can do something doesn't mean you should.
5. A haunting ending without easy answers The ending is what resonates the most. When the Thasians appear to reclaim Charlie, the story abruptly reframes what we’ve seen. These beings, who gifted him with the abilities that ensured his survival, now realize that allowing him to reintegrate into human society was a terrible mistake. Taking him back and permanently removing him from his own people is their solution.
Charlie makes agonizing last pleas. He sounds more like a scared adolescent, who has finally realized what he is going to lose, rather than a villain. He begs to stay without music or festivities while the crew looks on in shock and helplessness. Charlie is too dangerous to be on board, and it is tragic to send a young child into total seclusion to keep others safe.
That refusal to offer a clean, morally satisfying resolution is a big part of why “Charlie X” still resonates. There is no clever loophole that saves everyone. The episode suggests that sometimes, the best available choice is still tragic, and it trusts viewers enough to end on that unresolved, uneasy note.
Taken together, these elements make “Charlie X” a great 60th anniversary rewatch. It’s not comfortable and not always graceful, but it is bold in the questions it asks about power, growing up, and the cost of protecting a community from one of its own.
